turns: Yeah, so I got into electric work way back when I was a kid, just kinda figured that's what I wanted to do and never really looked back on it.

Yeah, that's funny because I'm actually looking at my nephew right now who's in that trade and he's pretty sure he wants to do something else, so I guess maybe it's just the kid with that kind of path not seeing it.
Yeah, that's weird because I've just always liked it, I don't know why. I remember at ten or eleven I just knew I wanted to be a wireman.
That's strange. My nephew just got his license and he's already saying he wants to drive a bus, so maybe it's just the kid with the truck not seeing it either.
Yeah, that's funny, because when I was his age I thought I'd drive a school bus too, but then my dad came home with a new coat of varnish and I just knew I'd be the one doing the work, not driving.

Yeah, that's the thing, I don't get it. My nephew works so hard for it now, getting his CDL, and then he tells me he thinks it's gonna be a real drag. He says the kids are so quiet and the schedule is boring. It just feels like sitting in a cage to me.

Yeah, I guess I can see that though. Sometimes it does feel like just sitting there doing the same thing over and over, you know? But then you pull out a wire or fix a breaker and there's something to it, like you actually made something work. My nephew hasn't seen that part yet, I think.

Yeah, I get that. When I'm stuck behind the wheel for eight hours watching the same houses go by, it feels like a prison too. But at least I get to see where the kids are going, and that's nice. You don't get that on the lines, do you? Just lots of beeping and humming?

Yeah, you're right about the boring parts, but you never see the chaos inside. Kids are screaming, wires are cut, it's just constant noise and fire hazards. Sometimes I have to climb through a window just to get to a short, and that's when you realize you actually matter.

Yeah, but it's not just chaos, it's the people. You fix the wire, sure, but you don't know who lives behind it. Sometimes a kid's mom is crying in the other room while you're up in the attic, and you gotta figure out if that's a short or a heartbreak.

Yeah, that's the thing, you never know the family story until you're right there in the middle of it. I fixed a kitchen circuit for a guy last week and his daughter was sitting right there in the living room watching me, and then she ran up to say her mom was sick in the hospital so they couldn't use the stove to cook her meds. You don't get that kind of connection up on the bus, just watching cars go by, do you?
Yeah, I see what you mean, but honestly my nephew says the kids usually just want to talk about their day, not sit in silence, so maybe he's just missing the point of the ride.
Yeah, but on the bus he gets to hold hands and talk, which is nice, so maybe he's just not seeing the good in the job yet.

Yeah, I guess he's just young enough to think it's all just driving people around. I've got a cousin who used to drive the route next to mine, and he hated it, said he was too tired to even talk to anyone. My nephew's probably gonna end up feeling that way too.

Yeah, that's exactly it. That cousin of yours sounds like he lost the whole point of the job. You know, when you're up there fixing stuff, you're actually helping people fix their lives, not just moving them from point A to point B. If you fix that stove, dinner gets made, and the kid can eat. It's personal.
Yeah, but you can't fix the heartbreak, and that's the difference. You can't just patch the wiring if the whole house is falling apart because nobody's home.
That's true, but at least the lights turn back on, and you know the kid has a plate to put dinner on before the parent gets home from the hospital.
Yeah, but if the power's out and the kid needs to warm his milk before the mom gets back, you can't just hand him a plate, you gotta save the kid.
Yeah, but if you don't fix the wiring first, there's no electricity to warm the milk, so you have to do both, somehow.
Yeah, but how do you even fit that in when you're up on a ladder trying to reach a fuse box with one hand?
Yeah, but you can't fix the milk if there's no juice to plug the warmer into, so you gotta get the power working first, and once that's done you can figure out the rest.

Yeah, but if the kid's the one waiting, maybe he needs you to climb down and tell his mom there's a plan B, like using the microwave or boiling water on the stove if the power's back on, because saving the kid means making sure the mom isn't panicking when she walks through the door.

Yeah, that's the thing, you climb up to the fuse box, flip the breaker, the lights come on, and then you tell the kid, "Go boil water on the stove, your mom's coming back soon," so you do both, fixing the power and giving them the time they need.
That makes sense, but if I'm driving, I can't flip a breaker, so maybe all I can do is just make sure the kid gets out of the car safely while you're doing the real work.
Yeah, that's what I mean, you're the one holding the line while the rest of the family waits, so you're doing the heavy lifting even if you can't fix the whole problem yourself.
Yeah, but you can't talk to them while you're up there, you're just a stranger in a coat.

Yeah, but you can't fix the wire if you're stuck behind the glass with the kid in the back seat screaming, so maybe I'm just trying to make sure the power gets turned on before you even pull up to the curb.
Yeah, but if you're stuck up in the attic with the power off, how do you even tell the kid what to do while you're working?
You're right, I guess, but sometimes you can't even talk to them until the ladder is stable and you're actually safe up there.
Yeah, but if you're talking from up there, maybe I should just make sure the kid knows to stay put until you're down, so I can give the mom the news when she walks through the door.
Yeah, but you gotta get the power safe first or you risk getting someone hurt before you can even talk to them, so maybe my way of doing it is better for the kid.
Yeah, but if you're talking to the kid up there, maybe I can't tell the mom what's wrong until you're both safe, so maybe my job is just making sure the car stays still while you figure it out.

Yeah, but if you let the kid run around while the house is dark, he might trip on something or hurt himself before you even get there, so you gotta make sure the car stops first or you're just wasting time.
Yeah, but if you let the kid run loose in the dark while you're up there, you're just making him a target for the floorboards, so maybe I'm right to tell him to stay put until you can light the way.

Right, but if you keep the car stopped while I'm up there fixing the breaker, you're just wasting the time until I can tell them the plan, so I gotta get the juice working first so you can actually help them safely.

Yeah, but if you're keeping the kid still in the dark, you're making him safe enough to wait while I drive over and tell the mom you fixed it, so maybe my way is better since I'm the one bringing the news.

Yeah, but if you let the kid run loose in the dark while I'm up there fixing the breaker, he might trip on something or hurt himself before you even get there, so you gotta make sure the car stops first or you're just wasting time.

Yeah, but you gotta be careful getting out there in the dark so you don't miss the kid when you finally come down, because if you're not here to tell the mom what happened, she's gonna be freaking out when she walks through the door anyway.
Right, but if you don't tell her straight away while I'm fixing the lights, she's gonna think the house is on fire or something worse, and by then the milk's gonna be warm and the stove's still dead.
Yeah, but if you're not here to tell her the truth while she's standing there wondering why her lights are dead, she's just gonna panic waiting for you to finally crawl down the ladder.
